generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology you paraphrase far more often than you quote: findings are usually reported in your own words rather than quoted directly. That makes one rule easy to forget - a paraphrased finding still needs an in-text reference, the author and year, because the finding is the researchers' even when the words are yours. Accuracy matters too: build each APA reference from its parts rather than pasting one in, where errors and inconsistencies creep in.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students report the same study's finding, in their own words, in an essay.

Tom rewrites the finding as a neat sentence of his own and moves on, giving no reference because he has not quoted directly. The sentence reads as Tom's own point. But the finding is the researchers', and with no reference it is now presented as Tom's - the very thing referencing exists to prevent.

Amara also puts the finding into her own words, but adds an in-text reference to the authors and year. When she does quote a definition directly, the exact words go in quotation marks with a page number. Paraphrase or quote, the finding is credited to the researchers either way.

Both students paraphrased accurately. Only Amara recognised that a paraphrased finding needs a reference just as a quotation does.
generatedProse.summary: Referencing accurately in psychology comes down to two habits: reference whenever you use a finding - when you paraphrase, which is most of the time, as well as when you quote - and build each APA reference carefully rather than pasting in a ready-made one. You can now explain when an in-text reference is needed, tell an accurate reference from a flawed one, and choose the accurate way to reference a quotation or a paraphrase. With the purpose, the parts and the practice in place, you are ready to reference your own psychology work with confidence.

check.body: In the worked example, what was the problem with Tom's paraphrase?

items.text: The finding was the researchers', but with no reference it read as Tom's own.
The paraphrase was not written clearly enough.
He quoted too many of the authors' exact words.
The paraphrase was shorter than the original.

feedback.correct: That's right. An unreferenced paraphrase presents the researchers' finding as Tom's own.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what was missing from Tom's paraphrase.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Tom's paraphrase had no reference, so the researchers' finding read as his own. Clarity, quoting and length were not the problem.
